1. The present government appeal under Section 378 (3) CrPC has been filed against the impugned judgement and order dated 10.7.2018 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge/ FTC-1, Aligarh in S.T. No. 702 of 2011, arising out of Case Crime No.816 of 2010 under Sections 363, 366 and 376 IPC,
Police Station Delhi Gate, District Aligarh, whereby accused-respondents were acquitted.
2. We have heard Shri Ashish Tiwari, learned AGA appearing for the State - appellant and perused the trial court record.

sentences.text: 3. The prosecution story, in nutshell, as narrated in the F.I.R. lodged by the informant Rashid son of Mahfooz Khan, is that on 22.11.2010 her sister aged about 14 years was missing while she had gone to ease her and a missing report was given at police station concerned.
Subsequently, he came to know that one Imran enticed away her with the assistance of Irfan, Gufran, Rehan Gunebahar and Mazhar Ali.
On the basis of written report of the informant, F.I.R. was lodged for the offence under Sections 363 and 366 IPC and investigation started.
4. After recovery, the victim was medically examined and on the basis of the statement of the victim recorded under Section 164 CrPC, offence under Section 376 IPC was added into the matter.
After completing necessary formalities, the Investigating Officer submitted charge sheet against accused/respondents.
After submission of charge sheet, the case was committed to the Court of Sessions.

Charges under Sections 363, 366 and 376 IPC against accused Imran and Gufran and under Sections 363 and 366 IPC against accused Rehan were framed by the Court of Sessions to which they denied and insisted to be tried.
Trial started and during trial, the prosecution produced as many as five prosecution witnesses.
In addition to this, the prosecution also produced a number of documents, which were duly exhibited and proved.

5. After conclusion of the prosecution evidence, incriminating evidence and circumstances were put to the accused persons in their statements under Section 313 CrPC wherein they alleged the prosecution evidence to be false and fabricated.
They also alleged their false implication in the matter due to animosity of Gram Pradhan election.

The learned Additional Sessions Judge, Aligarh after thrashing the evidence and critically analysing it acquitted the accused respondents from the charges framed against them and they were set at liberty.
6. Aggrieved with the said judgement and order, the instant Government Appeal under Section 378 (3) Cr.P.C. on behalf of the Sate / appellant has been preferred.

7. Learned State Counsel relying upon the prosecution witnesses submitted that the trial court has failed to appreciate the evidence in its true perspective and acquitted the accused respondents by wrong appreciation of the evidence available on record.
Findings recorded by the trial court in the impugned judgment and order are perverse and against the record warranting interference by this Court.

8. Since this is the appeal against acquittal, it will be relevant to note the principles of law laid down by the Apex Court with regard to the appreciation of evidence and approach to be adopted while dealing with an appeal against acquittal.
9. In Jafarudheen and others vs. State of Kerala, 2022 SCC Online SC 495, reiterating the principle on the subject the Hon'ble Apex Court reminded to the Courts as extracted below:

entities.text: Jafarudheen and others vs. State of Kerala, 2022 SCC Online SC 495
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "25. While dealing with an appeal against acquittal by invoking Section 378 of the Cr.PC, the Appellate Court has to consider whether the Trial Court's view can be termed as a possible one, particularly when evidence on record has been analyzed.
The reason is that an order of acquittal adds up to the presumption of innocence in State Of U.P. vs Imran And 2 Ors.

entities.text: State Of U.P. vs Imran And 2 Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
on 12 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/88484577/
2 favour of the accused.
Thus, the Appellate Court has to be relatively slow in reversing the order of the Trial Court rendering acquittal.
Therefore, the presumption in favour of the accused does not get weakened but only strengthened.

Such a double presumption that enures in favour of the accused has to be disturbed only by thorough scrutiny on the accepted legal parameters."
10.

In Mohan alias Srinivas alias Seena alias Tailor Seena vs. State of Karnataka, (2022) 12 SCC 619,
the Hon'ble Apex Court held as hereunder:
"20.

entities.text: Mohan alias Srinivas alias Seena alias Tailor Seena vs. State of Karnataka, (2022) 12 SCC 619
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Section 378 CrPC enables the State to prefer an appeal against an order of acquittal Section 384 CrPC speaks of the powers that can be exercised by the Appellate Court.

When the trial court renders its decision by acquitting the accused,
presumption of innocence gathers strength before the Appellate Court.
As a consequence, the onus on the prosecution becomes more burdensome as there is a double presumption of innocence.

Certainly, the Court of first instance has its own advantages in delivering its verdict, which is to see the witnesses in person while they depose The Appellate Court is expected to involve itself in a deeper, studied scrutiny of not only the evidence before it, but is duty bound to satisfy itself whether the decision of the trial court is both possible and plausible view
When two views are possible, the one taken by the trial court in a case of acquittal is to be followed on the touchstone of liberty along with the advantage of having seen the witnesses.

Article 21 of the Constitution of India also aids the accused after acquittal in a certain way,
though not absolute.
Suffice it is to state that the Appellate Court shall remind itself of the role required to play, while dealing with a case of an acquittal.

11. In Atley v. State of U.P., 1955 Cri. LJ 1653, the approach of the appellate court while considering a judgment of acquittal was discussed and it was observed that unless the appellate court comes to the conclusion that the judgment of the acquittal was perverse, it could not set aside the same.
12.

entities.text: Atley v. State of U.P., 1955 Cri. LJ 1653
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Bannareddy v. State of Karnataka, (2018) 5 SCC 790, has considered the power and jurisdiction of the High Court while interfering in an appeal against acquittal and held as under :
"26.

entities.text: Bannareddy v. State of Karnataka, (2018) 5 SCC 790
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The High Court should not have re-appreciated the evidence in its entirety,
especially when there existed no grave infirmity in the findings of the trial Court.

There exists no justification behind setting aside the order of acquittal passed by the trial Court, especially when the prosecution case suffers from several contradictions and infirmities".
13.

In Ramesh Babulal Doshi vs. State of Gujarat, (1996) 9 SCC 225, the Hon'ble Apex Court observed vis-a-vis the powers of an appellate court while dealing with a judgment of acquittal and held like this :

3 "7. While sitting in judgment over an acquittal the appellate court is first required to seek an answer to the question whether the findings of the trial court are palpably wrong, manifestly erroneous or demonstrably unsustainable.
If the appellate court answers the above question in the negative the order of acquittal is not to be disturbed.

Conversely, if the appellate court holds, for reasons to be recorded, that the order of acquittal cannot at all be sustained in view of any of the above infirmities it can then and then only reappraise the evidence to arrive at its own conclusions."

14. In the light of the submissions made by learned counsel for both the sides, we have carefully gone through the evidence available on record, analysis and appreciation thereof and conclusion arrived at by the trial court in the impugned judgment and order dated 10.7.2018.
15. The learned trial court proceeded to scrutinize the evidence on record to find out the truth behind the story.
The prosecution mainly relied upon the testimony of the PW-1, the prosecutrix.

She states that on 22.11.2010 at 8.00 p.m. while she had gone to ease her in the field, accused Irfan and Farukh covered her with cloth and shut her mouth and thereafter carried her at Bamba Pulia where a Car was already standing.
They put her into the Car in which Gufran, Imran and Zaheer were already present.
They rushed for Delhi and on the way accused Rehan, Farukh and Zaheer got off the vehicle.
Accused Imran and Gufran carried her to Delhi where she was kept in a room of the house and both of them committed rape with her against her will.

She has also stated that accused Imran and Gufran carried her from Delhi to Aligarh where police held her and brought at P.S. Delhi Gate where her statement was recorded and she was medically examined.
Thereafter, she was handed over to her father and aunt (Bua).
Her statement under Section 164 CrPC was also recorded wherein she supported the prosecution case.
16. To support the testimony of PW-1, PW-2 - Rashid, the informant, has also been examined, who corroborates the prosecution case.

He further proves written report as Ext. ka-2.
17. PW-3 Dr. Amita Rani Gupta medically examined the victim.
She has stated before the Court that no external injury was seen over the body of the prosecutrix.
Hymen was old torn but no mark of injury was found over her private part.
In the supplementary pathology report, no semen was found.
She has further stated that no definite opinion about rape with the victim could be given.
In her opinion the age of the victim was about 19 years.

She has proved the medical report as Ext. ka-3 and supplementary report as Ext. ka-4.
18.
PW-4 S.S.I. Mohd. Aslam is the second Investigating Officer of this case and prior to him as per his deposition I.O. Prem Singh was investigating the matter.
This witness proves the proceedings of investigation and states that after collecting sufficient evidence charge sheet Ext. ka-5 was filed against accused persons.
19. PW-5 Constable Virendra Kumar is the secondary witness for Head Moharrir Samrath Singh and H.C.P. Prem Singh and proved the chick report and G.D. as Ext. ka-6 and Ext. ka-7 respectively.

4 20.

sentences.text: The accused respondents in their statement under Section 313 CrPC claimed the entire prosecution evidence to be false and fabricated.
They also alleged their false implication due to animosity of Gram Pradhan election.

21. The main contention raised by the learned counsel for the State / appellant is that the prosecutrix in this case is a minor girl and being a minor girl, her testimony stands upon a distinguished footing.
It is also submitted that the legal parameters are settled in the matter where the credibility of the evidence of minor prosecutrix is under question.
It is vehemently submitted that normally the evidence of the prosecutrix must be relied upon and it should not be visualised with a suspicious vision.
22. In the light of the aforesaid submissions, we proceed to scrutinize the evidence on record.

23. The learned trial court has given a categorical finding that the prosecution has not explained the inordinate delay in lodging the F.I.R. in this matter and the conduct of the prosecutrix itself raises a question upon the credibility of the prosecution case.
The trial court, at the outset, examined the issue of minority of the victim.
As per the prosecution case she was aged about 14 years at the time of the incident.
The medical examination report Ext. ka-3 and the supplementary report Ext. ka-4 have also been perused by the trial court.
The learned trial court pointed out that no educational testimonials have been produced by the prosecution to ascertain the age of the victim whereas she deposes that she had studied in Class-8.

In the absence of school papers following the preferences embodied in Rule 12 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Rules, 2007, the learned trial court proceeded to examine the medical report available on record for the sake of ascertainment of the age of the victim.

entities.text: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Rules, 2007
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The victim has been medically examined by the team of doctors and the Chief Medical Officer, Aligarh has issued a certificate wherein the age of the prosecutrix was mentioned as about 18 years.
It is significant that the said medical report has not been countered by the prosecution.

Interestingly, the informant - PW-2 in his cross-examination admits that at the time of lodging the F.I.R. the victim was aged about 19 years but by some inadvertent mistake it was mentioned as 14 years in the F.I.R.

On the basis of the evidence available on record, the learned trial court reached a logical conclusion that at the time of the occurrence the prosecutrix, in any circumstance, was not below the age of 18 years and she was major.
The said finding of the learned trial court diminishes the charge under Section 363 IPC against the accused respondents.
24. This Court also finds that no municipal record was also available before the Court in order to ascertain the age of the victim.
25. The learned trial court also emphasised a very relevant fact which emerges out from the statements made by PW-1 prosecutrix and PW-2, informant.
Both the aforesaid witnesses deposed before the Court that there are three toilets in their house.
The ladies of the family use the said toilets and none of them goes out to get ease.

In these circumstances, a natural question arises, as the trial court also pointed out that inspite of having three toilets in the house, which were in use,
what was the reason the prosecutrix went out to the field in the night at 8.00 p.m. to get ease.

From the above, it infers that the prosecutrix was a consenting party to the relation made with her by the State Of U.P. vs Imran And 2 Ors. on 12 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/88484577/
5 accused persons and her consent is also inferred from her further conduct.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 26. Appearing as PW-1, the prosecutrix in her examination-in-chief, no doubt, deposes against the accused persons Imran and Gufran and makes a statement against them for kidnapping and committing rape with her, but however in her cross-examination her credibility is shattered.

She admits in her cross-examination that she was taken by accused Imran in a Van to Delhi and she was threatened for life by tamancha by accused Gufran and she had disclosed this fact to the I.O. but the said fact is not found in her statement recorded under Section 161 CrPC.
She further admits that in Delhi she was kept in a room of a house where she was kept for two days and during this period she did not even go to get ease nor she used water in any work.
Subsequently, she was taken to Aligarh and rape was committed with her at Delhi and Aligarh as well.
Further, she states that she came back to Aligarh in a public bus and she came to the bus stand by an Auto and found a public crowd there.
The house, where she was kept, was at a public place and the members of public and several persons were moving in front of the said house and she travelled for about one hour in the Auto.
She further admits that she came back to Aligarh from Delhi with Imran and was held by the police alongwith Imran and subsequently was given in the supurdgi of her mother by the police.
She fairly admits that she never complained to anyone during her journey for the offence which was committed with her.

The learned trial court elaborately discussed the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2 and found that the unnatural conduct of the prosecutrix was very relevant in the matter, which made the whole prosecution story as false.

27. Concurring with the trial court's finding, we are also of the considered view that it is not plausible at all that the young prosecutrix was kidnapped from an open place and was taken to Aligarh and Delhi by some public transport and she was also kept in confinement in some aabadi place but she never made any noise, alarm or complaint of kidnapping her and also for the physical assault made by the accused persons with her to any person at any public place.

28. The evidence rendered by the prosecution is not natural at all and the findings arrived at by the learned trial court in the impugned judgment and order in connection with the reliability of the deposition of PW-1 the victim, are found correct.

We find the prosecution evidence as shaky,
cursory, unnatural and improbable.

29. It is notable that in a sexual offence case the evidence of the prosecutrix has got a distinguished place which must be paid respect to but since the same does not inspire confidence and is not reliable and consistent, the trial court was never bound to act upon the testimony of such an unreliable witness.

30. In Mohd. Ali @ Guddu vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2015) 7 Supreme Court Cases 272, it has been held by the Hon'ble Apex Court that there can be no iota of doubt that a conviction can be based upon sole testimony of prosecutrix, even without corroboration, if it is unimpeachable and beyond reproach.

entities.text: Mohd. Ali @ Guddu vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2015) 7 Supreme Court Cases 272
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In the said case considering the entire circumstances of the case and particularly the testimony of the prosecutrix it was found that it leave a mark of doubt to treat the testimony of the prosecutrix as so natural and truthful to inspire confidence and it was concluded with certitude that the evidence of prosecutrix was not of such quality which can be placed reliance.
State Of U.P. vs Imran And 2 Ors. on 12 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/88484577/
6 31.

entities.text: State Of U.P. vs Imran And 2
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Apex Court in Samsul Haque v. State of Assam, (2019) 18 SCC 161 held that the judgment of acquittal, where two views are possible, should not be set aside, even if view formed by appellate court may be a more probable one, interference with acquittal can only be justified when it is based on a perverse view.

entities.text: Samsul Haque v. State of Assam, (2019) 18 SCC 161
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 32. In view of the aforesaid discussions, we are of the view that the learned trial Court has given logical and plausible findings in the impugned judgement in conformity with the evidence on record and has rightly concluded that the prosecution has miserably failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The judgment and order of the trial court under judicious scrutiny is just and proper and carries no perversity therein, hence it does not warrant any interference by this Court.
The reasoning adopted by the learned Trial Judge is based upon proper application of judicial mind.
No illegality, infirmity or perversity is found in the impugned judgment and order and it needs no interference by this Court.
33. Thus, the application moved by the appellant - State to grant leave to appeal for the reasons discussed here-in-above is not liable to be allowed and the said prayer is refused.
Re : Government Appeal 34.
Since the application for grant of leave to appeal has been disallowed, the government appeal is dismissed at this stage.
